title: How much is it? — at the market
goal: Ask prices, name weights and quantities, pay and receive change in forints.
bekal: ask the price with *mennyibe kerül* and understand the answer
order by weight and container: *egy kiló*, *fél kiló*, *egy üveg*
pay, work out the change, and choose between cash and card

dialogs.title: Dialogue — A piacon
dialogs.intro: The covered market at Hunyadi tér, Saturday morning. Budi stands in front of a table piled with red peppers.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Jó napot! Mennyibe kerül a paprika?
lines.id: Good afternoon! How much are the peppers?
lines.literal: good day! how-much-into it-costs the pepper?

lines.speaker: Árus:
lines.id: Five hundred forints a kilo. Very fresh.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: And how much are the tomatoes?

lines.speaker: Árus:
lines.id: The tomatoes are six hundred and forty forints.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Kérek egy kiló paradicsomot és fél kiló almát.
lines.id: I'd like a kilo of tomatoes and half a kilo of apples.
lines.literal: I-ask a kilo tomato-OBJ and half kilo apple-OBJ.

lines.speaker: Árus:
lines.text: Melyik almát? Ez édes, az savanyú.
lines.id: Which apples? These are sweet, those are sour.
lines.literal: which apple-OBJ? this sweet, that sour.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Az édeset kérem. Valami mást nem kérek.
lines.id: I'd like the sweet ones. Nothing else.
lines.literal: the sweet-OBJ I-ask-it. something other-OBJ not I-ask.

lines.speaker: Árus:
lines.id: Fine. How much will it be? I'll work it out in a moment.

lines.speaker: Árus:
lines.id: It comes to one thousand two hundred forints in total.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Here you are, two thousand forints.

lines.speaker: Árus:
lines.text: Nyolcszáz a visszajáró. Köszönöm szépen, viszlát!
lines.id: Eight hundred is your change. Thank you very much, goodbye!
lines.literal: eight-hundred the change. I-thank nicely, goodbye!

notes: **Mennyibe kerül?** literally means "into how much does it cost". The construction is odd and not worth taking apart; learn it whole. A shorter form is just as polite: *Mennyi?* or *Mennyi lesz?*

**Ötszáz forint kilója** uses the possessive ending from Unit 5: literally "five hundred forints its-kilo". This is the standard way to give a price per unit, and you will hear it at every market stall.

**Forint never takes a plural.** *ötszáz forint*, *kétezer forint* — following the rule from Units 3 and 6: after a number, the noun stays singular. The abbreviation is **Ft**, written **after** the number: 1,200 Ft.

**Fél kiló, másfél kiló.** *Fél* means half, and *másfél* means one and a half — literally "other half". English has no word that short for "one and a half", and once you get used to it you will miss it.

**Az édeset kérem** shows two things at once. First, an adjective can stand alone as a noun: *az édes* = "the sweet one". Second, it then takes the object ending too: *az édeset*. Note also *kérem*, not *kérek* — the apples are now specific, so it is clear which ones. The rule waits in Unit 11.
**Lesz is the future of van.** *Mennyi lesz?* = "how much will it be?". It is the only Hungarian verb with a future form of its own; every other verb uses a different method, covered in Unit 20.

after: Note *kerülnek* in the second row: when the goods are plural, the verb is plural too. Getting it wrong is not fatal, but fixing it costs nothing.

*Olcsóbb* is the "-er" form of *olcsó*, built with the ending *-bb*. Comparison is covered fully in Unit 16; for now these three forms are enough: *olcsóbb* (cheaper), *jobb* (better), *nagyobb* (bigger).

grammars.title: Weights, quantities and containers
body: They all behave like numbers: the noun after them stays singular, and the object ending attaches to **the noun**, not to the unit.
after: **The deka is the most typically Hungarian unit.** One *deka* is ten grams, so *tíz deka* means a hundred grams. At the butcher's and the cheese counter, Hungarians almost never say grams — they say deka, and a beginner who asks for "száz gramm" immediately sounds like a foreigner.
Note once more where the object ending goes: *egy kiló almá**t***, not *egy kiló**t** alma*. The unit stays attached to the number; the thing acted on is still the noun.

blocks.text: *Paprika* in Hungary means two things at once: the fresh pepper sold at the market, and the red powder that gives *gulyás* its color. If you want the powder, say *őrölt paprika* (ground paprika) or just point — Hungarian market sellers are very used to translating hand gestures.

blocks.title: Forints in practice
items: Coins: 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200 Ft. Banknotes: 500, 1,000, 2,000, 5,000, 10,000, 20,000 Ft. The 20,000 note is often refused at small stalls, so keep some mid-size notes.

Cash totals at the till are **rounded to the nearest multiple of five**, because 1 and 2 forint coins are no longer in circulation. Card payments are not rounded — so the figure on the receipt and the amount you pay can differ by a few forints, and that is normal.
At the market, cards are not always accepted. Say *Kártyával lehet?* **before** the seller starts weighing.
